concepts.name: Dyarchy: Mechanism and Division of Subjects at Provincial Level
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'Reserved' subjects (administered by Governor with Executive Council) vs 'Transferred' subjects (administered by Ministers responsible to legislature)
Specific examples of reserved subjects (law & order, finance, land revenue) vs transferred subjects (education, public health, agriculture) — UPSC frequently tests misclassification
Why dyarchy was criticized as unworkable: finance remained reserved, crippling transferred subjects
Contrast with dyarchy's abolition under Government of India Act 1935, where it was shifted to Centre

concepts.name: Montagu Declaration of 1917: Context and Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: Exact wording: 'increasing association of Indians in every branch of the administration' and 'gradual development of self-governing institutions' — UPSC traps on the word 'gradual' vs 'immediate'
Distinction between Montagu Declaration (1917) and Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) — different documents, different years
Role of Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy) — who held which office is a common trap
Why it was considered the first explicit acknowledgment of 'responsible government' as a goal, yet fell short of dominion status demand

concepts.name: Bicameralism at the Centre: Council of State and Legislative Assembly
key_dimensions: Introduction of bicameralism at the central level for the first time — Upper House (Council of State) vs Lower House (Central Legislative Assembly)
Composition differences: Council of State had 60 members (27 elected), Legislative Assembly had 145 members (105 elected) — numerical traps in UPSC
Distinction from earlier Imperial Legislative Council (single chamber under Morley-Minto 1909)
Limitations: Viceroy could certify bills, summon/prorogue/dissolve — legislature lacked real sovereignty

concepts.name: Communal Representation: Extension and Entrenchment
key_dimensions: Morley-Minto 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims; Montagu-Chelmsford extended it to Sikhs, Europeans, Anglo-Indians, and Indian Christians — UPSC tests which communities were added when
Concept of 'double determination': communal electorates plus reservation of seats — how these two mechanisms interacted
Nationalist critique: communal representation deepened divisions vs British justification of protecting minorities
Contrast with later Communal Award 1932 and Poona Pact 1932 — trajectory of communal representation

concepts.name: Franchise and Electoral Provisions under the 1919 Act
key_dimensions: Franchise was limited and property/tax-based — approximately 10% of population got voting rights, not universal suffrage
Differential franchise for provincial vs central legislatures — provincial had broader franchise than central
Women's franchise: left to provincial discretion — Madras was first province to grant women voting rights (1921)
Comparison with Morley-Minto (nominated/limited elected) vs 1919 (expanded elected element) vs 1935 (14% franchise)

concepts.name: Provincial Legislative Councils: Composition and Elected Majority
key_dimensions: For the first time, elected members formed a majority in provincial councils — a significant departure from Morley-Minto where official majority was retained
Governor's special powers: could override council decisions on reserved subjects — undermining the elected majority's significance
Variation in council sizes across provinces — Bengal, Bombay, Madras had larger councils
Distinction between the elected majority in provincial councils vs the still-restricted central legislature

concepts.name: Secretary of State for India: Changed Financial Status
key_dimensions: Pre-1919: Secretary of State's salary paid from Indian revenues (Indian taxpayer funded British oversight) — a major grievance
Post-1919: Secretary of State's salary shifted to British Exchequer — significance as symbolic concession
Retained superintendence, direction, and control over Indian Government — power not substantively reduced
Comparison with Government of India Act 1935 where Secretary of State's powers were further modified

concepts.name: High Commissioner for India: New Office Created
key_dimensions: New office created in London to handle commercial and business functions previously managed by Secretary of State
Distinction: High Commissioner handled trade/commercial matters; Secretary of State retained political/constitutional control — UPSC traps on role overlap
Appointed by Government of India (not Crown) — significance for accountability
Precursor to modern High Commissioner concept; contrast with Agent-General created later

concepts.name: Central Public Service Commission: Genesis
key_dimensions: 1919 Act provided for the first statutory basis for a Public Service Commission at the Centre
Actual establishment of Central Public Service Commission in 1926 — gap between provision (1919) and implementation (1926) is a UPSC trap
Lee Commission (1924) recommendation that accelerated its establishment
Distinction from Federal Public Service Commission under 1935 Act and eventual UPSC under 1950 Constitution

concepts.name: Devolution Rules 1920: Operationalizing Dyarchy
key_dimensions: Devolution Rules were the subsidiary legislation that actually divided subjects into central, provincial-reserved, and provincial-transferred — the Act itself did not list all subjects
Finance as the critical fault line: provincial governments had transferred subjects but no independent financial control
Governor's power to restore a transferred subject to reserved category — the 'takeback' provision that made dyarchy fragile
How Devolution Rules differed conceptually from later lists (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent) under 1935 Act

concepts.name: Indian Legislature's Powers vs Viceroy's Special Powers
key_dimensions: Viceroy could certify any bill refused by legislature — effectively a legislative veto that nullified elected majority
Governor-General's power to issue ordinances (Section 72) — bypassing legislature entirely
Budget: a portion was 'non-votable' (demand not subject to vote) — financial control remained restricted
Contrast with Westminster model where executive is fully accountable to legislature — exposing the 'responsible government' claim as hollow

concepts.name: Relationship Between 1919 Act and Rowlatt Act: Political Contradictions
key_dimensions: Both passed in 1919 — reforms and repression simultaneously, a key UPSC analytical theme
Rowlatt Act (March 1919) came before the Government of India Act (December 1919) — sequence matters
Nationalist response: Congress boycotted the reformed councils initially (later reversed by Swarajists in 1923)
How this contradiction shaped Gandhi's assessment of the reforms and launch of Non-Cooperation Movement 1920

concepts.name: Statutory Commission Provision (Section 84A): Built-in Review Mechanism
key_dimensions: 1919 Act itself mandated a Statutory Commission within 10 years to review the working of the reforms — unusual self-review clause
Simon Commission (1927) was the outcome — appointed 2 years early, entirely British, triggering the boycott
Why the all-British composition of Simon Commission violated the spirit (if not letter) of the Act
Chain: Simon Commission Report (1930) → Round Table Conferences → Government of India Act 1935

concepts.name: Congress and Moderates' Response: From Rejection to Partial Engagement
key_dimensions: Initial Congress position (1920 Nagpur session): boycott of reformed councils under Non-Cooperation Movement
Swarajist faction (C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru) reversed this in 1923 — 'responsive cooperation' strategy of entering councils to obstruct from within
Contrast with Moderates (Liberal Federation) who welcomed the reforms and participated from the start
UPSC trap: Non-Cooperation boycott was of legislatures AND courts AND schools — not just legislatures

concepts.name: Morley-Minto 1909 vs Montagu-Chelmsford 1919: Comparative Constitutional Evolution
key_dimensions: 1909: Nominated official majority retained at Centre; 1919: Elected majority in provinces but Centre still controlled
1909: Separate electorates for Muslims only; 1919: Extended to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, Indian Christians
1909: No dyarchy concept; 1919: Dyarchy introduced at provincial level
1909: No bicameralism at Centre; 1919: Bicameral central legislature introduced — most commonly tested structural comparison

concepts.name: Government of India Act 1919 vs Government of India Act 1935: Continuity and Breaks
key_dimensions: 1919: Dyarchy at provinces; 1935: Dyarchy shifted to Centre (never implemented) and provinces got full autonomy
1919: No Federal structure; 1935: All-India Federation proposed (with princely states) — never fully implemented
1919: Central Public Service Commission provision; 1935: Federal/Provincial PSCs established
Continuity: Both retained communal electorates, Viceroy's overriding powers, and Secretary of State's superintendence

concepts.name: Reforms and the 'Responsible Government' Debate: Promise vs Reality
key_dimensions: Montagu Declaration used 'responsible government' — but the Act created accountability only for transferred subjects in provinces, not at Centre

Difference between 'responsible government' (executive accountable to legislature) and 'representative government' (elected legislature without executive accountability) — 1919 gave the latter, not former
Annie Besant's Home Rule critique vs Moderates' acceptance — different benchmarks for 'responsible government'
Why Tilak called the reforms 'unworthy of England to offer and India to accept' — contextualizing the phrase for analytical questions

concepts.name: Indianization of Civil Services: Provisions and Limitations
key_dimensions: 1919 Act and subsequent Lee Commission (1924) set a target for Indianization of ICS and other services
Simultaneous recruitment in England and India for ICS — but English examination remained the primary route until 1935
Distinction between ICS (covenanted/superior) and Provincial Civil Services (uncovenanted) — Indianization was faster in lower services
UPSC trap: Indianization was a process, not an immediate outcome of the 1919 Act — full Indianization only post-Independence

concepts.name: Indian Council Advisory Body: Reduction in Powers
key_dimensions: Indian Council in London (created by Government of India Act 1858) was retained but its mandatory consultation was reduced
Secretary of State no longer required to consult Council on all matters — discretionary consultation weakened the check
Size of Council reduced from 15 to a range of 8-12 members
Eventual abolition of the India Council under Government of India Act 1935 — trajectory toward its elimination

concepts.name: Fiscal Relations and Budget Division: Central vs Provincial Finance
key_dimensions: 1919 reforms attempted separation of central and provincial finances — 'provincial settlement' concept
Heads of revenue assigned exclusively to Centre (customs, income tax) vs provinces (land revenue, excise) vs shared — UPSC tests specific assignments
Provincial governments could not raise loans without Centre's approval — fiscal autonomy remained curtailed
Contrast with 1935 Act's more elaborate federal finance provisions and the eventual Finance Commission under 1950 Constitution
